notes.b: Pollution is the release of substances or energy into the environment at a rate that harms living things or damages natural processes. It is usually grouped by where the harm happens: in the air, in water or through sound.
points: Air pollution: gases and particles released into the atmosphere, mainly from burning fossil fuels, industry, traffic and domestic fires.
Water pollution: harmful substances entering rivers, lakes, groundwater or the sea, from sewage, farming, industry and households.
Noise pollution: unwanted or excessive sound from traffic, construction, industry and household equipment.
Litter and land pollution: discarded waste on streets, in the countryside and in water, which harms wildlife and blocks drains.
notes.tip: When asked to name types of pollution, give air, water and noise, and for each give one cause and one effect. Do not mix a cause into the effect.

notes.b: Most air pollution comes from burning something, whether fuel in a power station, a car engine or a home fire. Each pollutant comes from a particular kind of burning, so it helps to link each gas to its source.
points: Carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide are released when fossil fuels such as coal, oil, peat and gas are burned for electricity, transport and home heating; sulphur dioxide comes especially from coal, oil and peat.
Nitrogen oxides are produced by vehicle engines and by any high-temperature combustion, because the heat makes nitrogen and oxygen in the air combine.
Carbon monoxide is produced by incomplete combustion (burning without enough oxygen), for example in poorly maintained or faulty boilers, stoves and vehicle exhausts.
Smoke and particulates (tiny solid specks in the air) come from solid fuels such as coal, wood and smoky turf burned in open fires and stoves, and from industry. Smoke and fog together form smog.
CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) released from old fridge refrigerants and foams, and from older aerosol sprays, destroy ozone in the upper atmosphere.
Methane, a greenhouse gas, is released from landfill and from farm animals.
Overuse of chemical sprays and cleaning products, and burning rubbish, add further pollutants to the air.
notes.tip: For emissions from burning fuels in the home, name the gas, its effect and one way to reduce it. CFCs are long banned in the EU, so write about them in the past tense for aerosols; old fridges can still hold them.

notes.b: Air pollutants cause three separate global problems, plus harm to health. Keep each cause with its own effect, because examiners mark the link between them.
points: Global warming and climate change: carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere, raising average temperatures and sea levels and changing weather patterns and crops.

Acid rain: sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rainwater to form acids, which lower the pH of soil and water, harm plants and fish, dissolve limestone and corrode metal and stone buildings.
Ozone depletion: CFCs break down ozone in the stratosphere (the upper atmosphere), so more harmful ultraviolet radiation reaches the earth's surface.
Health: particulates and smoke cause respiratory illness, aggravate asthma and place extra strain on the heart.
Carbon monoxide is a poison that stops the blood carrying oxygen. It has no smell, which is why carbon monoxide detectors are used in homes.
Smog and smoke reduce air quality and visibility.
notes.tip: Global warming, acid rain and ozone depletion are different problems. Carbon dioxide does not cause acid rain, CFCs are not the cause of global warming, acid rain does not damage the ozone layer, and carbon monoxide is a poison, not a main cause of global warming.

notes.b: Water pollution happens when waste from homes, farms and industry reaches rivers, lakes and the sea, often through drains and run-off (rainwater washing material off land).
points: Untreated or poorly treated sewage is discharged into rivers and the sea.
Fertiliser and slurry (liquid animal waste) are washed off farmland into waterways after heavy rain; together with sewage, these are the main sources of nutrients.
Industrial effluent (liquid waste), chemical waste and pesticides are dumped or washed into water.
Oil leaking from vehicles and heating oil tanks runs off into drains and streams.
Household chemicals, paint and oil poured down drains also reach waterways.
Phosphates in washing powders and detergents once entered waterways through household drains. EU rules now limit phosphorus in these detergents, so they are no longer the main source.
notes.tip: Mention phosphate detergents once, as a historical cause, beside fertiliser, slurry and sewage. Mark schemes still credit it.

notes.b: The best-known effect is eutrophication, where too many nutrients set off a chain of events that ends with a lake or river short of oxygen. Other pollutants harm wildlife and people directly.
points: Eutrophication: excess nitrates and phosphates feed rapid growth of algae, which forms an algal bloom on the water surface.
The bloom blocks light, so submerged plants die; when the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up dissolved oxygen.
Low oxygen levels kill fish and other aquatic life, leaving lakes and rivers depleted.
Toxic substances can accumulate up the food chain, because each animal eats many contaminated ones, affecting fish and birds that feed on contaminated organisms.
Chemical contamination of drinking water sources threatens human health and can leave water unfit to drink.
notes.tip: Eutrophication is caused by nitrates and phosphates (nutrients), not by toxic chemicals. Write the steps in order: bloom, light blocked, plants die, bacteria use up oxygen, fish die.

notes.h: Causes and effects of noise pollution
notes.b: Noise is sound that is unwanted or too loud. Loud or constant noise damages health as well as comfort.
points: Main sources: road and air traffic, construction and roadworks, industry, lawnmowers, music systems, televisions and alarms.
Noise is measured in decibels (dB), a logarithmic scale, so an increase of 10 dB represents roughly a tenfold increase in sound intensity.
Effects of persistent noise: stress, tension, headaches, disturbed sleep and insomnia.
Long-term exposure to loud sound causes permanent hearing damage.
Noise reduces concentration in schools and workplaces.
notes.tip: Learn the rule that 10 dB means about ten times the sound intensity; it is the only noise figure you need.

notes.b: Individual choices add up. Consumers can cut air, water and noise pollution at home, on the road and when shopping.
points: Air: walk, cycle, use public transport or share car journeys to reduce vehicle emissions.
Air: drive an electric, hybrid or low-emission vehicle, and keep tyres correctly inflated and the engine serviced to reduce fuel use and emissions.
Air: use smokeless fuels or renewable heat, such as heat pumps or solar, instead of smoky solid fuels, and do not burn rubbish.
Air: choose energy-efficient appliances so that less fossil fuel is burned to generate the electricity they use. Dispose of old fridges and freezers properly so that CFCs are not released.

Water: never pour paint, oil or chemicals down drains, use fertilisers and chemicals sparingly, and compost garden waste rather than burning it. Keep boilers and oil tanks maintained so they do not leak.
Noise: keep music and television volumes down, avoid noisy garden work at unsocial hours, maintain equipment, and use double glazing and sound insulation.
General: reduce, reuse and recycle, buy only what is needed, choose biodegradable or second-hand products, and avoid single-use packaging.
notes.tip: For three ways to reduce pollution, pick clear actions such as public transport, electric cars, smokeless fuel or renewables, efficient appliances, reuse and recycle, or careful use of chemicals.

notes.b: Individuals cannot solve pollution alone, so the State uses laws, a regulator and charges that make polluting more expensive.
points: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), set up under the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992, licenses large industrial and waste activities, monitors air and water quality and enforces environmental law.
The Waste Management Act 1996 (as amended) controls waste collection, movement and disposal, and gives local authorities and the EPA roles in promoting reduction, recycling and reuse.

Solid fuel regulations: the Air Pollution Act 1987 (Solid Fuels) Regulations 2022 ban the sale of smoky (bituminous) coal across the State from 31 October 2022 and restrict the retail sale of turf and of wet wood, to cut smoke and particulates from home heating. Local authorities enforce them.

Levies and taxes make polluting choices dearer: the landfill levy (a charge per tonne of waste sent to landfill, encouraging recycling and recovery), the plastic bag levy (since 2002) and a carbon tax on fossil fuels (introduced in 2010), which encourages energy efficiency and renewable alternatives.
Other clean-green schemes: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; Green Dot (Repak); WEEE take-back; EU Ecolabel; and, since 2024, the Re-turn deposit return scheme.
Support for renewable energy and home energy upgrades, with grants through the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), reduces the fossil fuel burned.
notes.tip: When asked for one government initiative, name it and give two points, for example the Waste Management Act 1996 or the solid fuel regulations.

keyTerms.definition: The release of substances or energy into the environment at a rate that harms living things or natural processes.
Nutrient enrichment of water by nitrates and phosphates, which causes excessive growth of algae.
A rapid growth of algae on the surface of water, which blocks light and can deplete the oxygen in the water.
Rainfall made acidic by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolving in it, which damages plants, water and buildings.
The rise in average temperatures caused by greenhouse gases trapping heat in the atmosphere.
The thinning of the ozone layer, mainly by CFCs, which allows more ultraviolet radiation to reach the earth.
Chlorofluorocarbon, a synthetic gas formerly used in refrigerants, aerosols and foams that destroys ozone.
A tiny solid particle or droplet in the air, such as soot or smoke, that can be inhaled.
The unit used to measure the loudness of sound on a logarithmic scale.
Liquid waste discharged from homes, farms or industry into a water body.

factCards.definition: It lowers the pH of soil and water, harming plants and fish; it corrodes metal and stone buildings; it damages forests.
Burning fossil fuels in power stations and homes; vehicle emissions; CFCs from old fridges and aerosols; smoke from solid fuels and industrial emissions.

factCards.term: Three effects of nutrient pollution in water
factCards.definition: Algal blooms cover the water surface; oxygen levels fall as the algae decompose; fish and other aquatic life die.

factCards.term: Four ways consumers can reduce air pollution
factCards.definition: Walk, cycle or use public transport; choose an electric or low-emission vehicle; use smokeless or renewable heat; avoid products containing CFCs.
Stress and headaches; disturbed sleep and insomnia; permanent hearing damage from long-term exposure.
Old refrigerators and freezers, through their refrigerant and foam insulation; some older aerosol sprays.
A landfill levy; restrictions on the sale of smoky coal; a carbon tax on fossil fuels.

factCards.term: Two effects of burning coal, oil and peat
factCards.definition: Sulphur dioxide that forms acid rain; carbon dioxide that adds to global warming.

questions.prompt: Name two types of pollution and state one effect of each on the environment.
questions.model: Two types, each correctly named, for example air, water or noise pollution. One effect for each: air pollution causes global warming, acid rain or ozone depletion; water pollution causes algal blooms, oxygen depletion and the death of fish and aquatic life; noise pollution causes stress, disturbed sleep and hearing damage. Each effect must be linked to the named type.

questions.prompt: Identify two types of pollution. For each, describe its main causes and two effects on the environment, and outline one way in which a consumer can reduce it.
questions.model: Two types, correctly named. For each type, two causes: for air pollution, burning fossil fuels for heating and transport, and CFCs from fridges and aerosols; for water pollution, sewage and farm run-off of fertiliser and slurry, and phosphates in detergents. For each type, two effects: for air pollution, global warming and acid rain; for water pollution, eutrophication with algal blooms and oxygen depletion that kills fish. A consumer reduction measure for each type, such as walking, cycling or using public transport, or using phosphate-free detergents and not pouring chemicals down drains.
